sentences.text: The genus Calsoyasuchus is known from a single incomplete skull that is unusually derived for an Early Jurassic crocodylomorph. This preserved skull is approximately 38.0 centimeters long and features a long, low shape that curves with both ends higher than the middle.

The left maxilla of the holotype skull — the specimen the species is based on — is more complete than the right and contains at least 29 teeth. A deep groove runs along the midline of the nasal and frontal bones, and unlike derived neosuchians, Calsoyasuchus possessed external antorbital fenestrae.
CT scanning revealed that Calsoyasuchus had a double-walled secondary palate similar to true crocodylians and pneumatic cavities.
Calsoyasuchus was formally described in 2002 by Ronald Tykoski and colleagues. Fossils were found in the Kayenta Formation on Navajo Nation land in Coconino County, Arizona.
Calsoyasuchus was a crocodylomorph that lived during the Early Jurassic period, specifically between 199.5 and 184.2 million years ago during the Sinemurian and Pliensbachian ages.
The Kayenta Formation during the Early Jurassic contained a diverse fauna including caecilians, frogs, turtles, multiple crocodylomorphs, pterosaurs, dinosaurs, and early mammal relatives.
A 2022 analysis suggested Calsoyasuchus is the sister group of Thalattosuchia.
